questions.question: What does the if err != nil pattern mean in Go?
questions.title: Checking errors explicitly
questions.direct_answer: `if err != nil` asks whether an operation returned a failure value. Inside that branch, code must make a concrete decision: handle the failure, translate it, add context and return it, or deliberately continue. When `err` is nil, the normal result can be used according to the function's contract.

interviewer_intent.testing: The basic control-flow contract and meaningful choices inside the error branch.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating the check as ceremonial boilerplate or using the result before it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect each branch to a specific caller policy instead of always returning unchanged errors.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A nil error conventionally means the operation succeeded.
A non-nil error moves execution onto an explicit failure path.
Check the error before using an all-or-nothing result.
Handle, translate, wrap, or return the error intentionally.
Keep the successful path flat with an early return when possible.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The `if err != nil` pattern is Go's ordinary explicit failure branch. A function returns an error value alongside its normal result; nil means the operation succeeded under that API's contract, while a non-nil value says the caller must decide what happens next.

For an all-or-nothing function, I check the error before using the result. For example, after `port, err := strconv.Atoi(text)`, invalid text produces zero and a non-nil error. Using `port` first could confuse a failed conversion with a legitimate zero value.

The body should express policy, not merely repeat syntax. A low-level helper may add the operation and return the error. A service may translate a known not-found category. A command may display it and choose an exit status. If the current layer cannot improve or recover from the failure, it normally propagates it rather than pretending it succeeded.

I usually use an early return so the successful path stays unindented: check, return on failure, then continue with the valid value. Some contracts allow partial values, such as `io.Reader`, so their documented ordering still applies. The pattern is simple, but its purpose is to make the failure decision visible exactly where the call occurs.

sections.title: Turn a returned value into visible control flow
sections.content:
The check is a branch over data. Unlike a hidden transfer of control, it appears in the same lexical path as the call. Reviewers can see whether a failure stops the operation, changes form, triggers a fallback, or is intentionally ignored.

Short declarations can limit the error variable to the branch when only the error matters. When the successful result is needed afterward, declare both results before the check and return early. Shape the scope around the data that survives.

sections.title: The explicit success and failure paths
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Call function] --> B{err is not nil?}
  B -- Yes --> C{Can this layer recover?}
  C -- Yes --> D[Handle or translate]
  C -- No --> E[Add useful context and return]
  B -- No --> F[Use the valid result]
```

questions.question: When should a Go function handle an error instead of returning it?
questions.title: Handle errors at the layer with policy
questions.direct_answer: A function should handle an error when it can recover, retry safely, choose a fallback, or translate the failure into its own boundary's result. If it cannot make a useful decision, it should usually add relevant context and return the error so a higher layer can apply policy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Separation of low-level facts from application policy.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Logging, wrapping, and returning the same failure repeatedly without any layer owning it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace one not-found error from storage through service to HTTP response.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Handle an error only where a meaningful recovery or translation exists.
Return failures that the current layer cannot resolve.
Add concise operation context while preserving useful identity.
Do not both log and return the same error at every layer.
Translate dependency errors at stable package or transport boundaries.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I handle an error at the lowest layer that has enough policy to make a useful decision. Handling means the function can genuinely recover, choose a safe fallback, retry an idempotent operation, translate the failure into its own domain, or produce the final response. A layer that cannot do any of those should normally return it.

For example, a repository may wrap a database miss as the service's documented `ErrUserNotFound`. The service cannot invent a user, so it returns that category. The HTTP handler owns transport policy and converts it to a 404 response. Each layer adds meaning only once.

When propagating, I add concise context such as `load profile: %w` if it identifies the failed operation. I preserve an underlying category only when callers are meant to depend on it. I avoid logging and returning the same error at every layer because the final logger then receives several duplicate entries for one incident.

The boundary changes when a fallback is part of correct behavior. A cache miss can be handled by loading the database, while a database outage usually must propagate. Retries need limits and should be safe for the operation. My rule is simple: facts travel upward as errors; the first layer with the right policy owns the final action.

sections.title: Error facts move upward until policy can act
sections.content:
Low-level code knows which operation failed but often cannot decide what the application should do. Boundary code knows whether the outcome becomes a retry, HTTP status, CLI message, metric, or process exit. Passing errors between those layers keeps responsibilities clear.

Translation creates a deliberate abstraction. A package can turn several database-specific not-found forms into one domain category, preventing transport code from importing storage details. Logging usually belongs where the request or job has enough context to be recorded once.

sections.title: One failure, one policy owner
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant DB as Database
  participant R as Repository
  participant S as Service
  participant H as HTTP handler
  DB-->>R: row missing
  R-->>S: wrap as ErrUserNotFound
  S-->>H: return domain error
  H->>H: errors.Is and write 404
```

questions.question: Why is ignoring a returned error with the blank identifier risky?
questions.title: The cost of discarding errors
questions.direct_answer: Assigning an error to `_` removes the only signal that an operation failed. The accompanying result may be a zero value, nil pointer, short write, or incomplete state that looks valid enough to continue. Ignore an error only when its contract proves the failure cannot matter, and make that decision visible.

interviewer_intent.testing: Recognition that discarding an error also discards state needed to interpret the result.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `_` to silence the compiler and allowing a later symptom to hide the original failure.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how a failed conversion yields a believable zero value and changes business behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `_` discards the error; it does not make the operation succeed.
A failure result may look like a valid zero value.
Ignored I/O errors can cause data loss or later panics.
Check and handle errors at the point where their meaning is clear.
If an error is intentionally irrelevant, document why the contract makes it safe.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The blank identifier deliberately throws a value away. If that value is an error, the program loses the information needed to decide whether the accompanying result is usable. Nothing about `_` retries the operation, supplies a fallback, or validates the result.

For example, `age, _ := strconv.Atoi("unknown")` gives `age` the zero value. Later code may treat that as a real age of zero and store incorrect data. The visible bug appears in validation or persistence, far away from the conversion that actually failed.

The damage can be worse around resources. Ignoring `os.Open` may leave a nil file value that causes a later panic. Ignoring write, flush, close, or transaction errors can lose data even when earlier work seemed successful. The first error is usually the clearest description of the cause.

There are narrow cases where an API contract guarantees the error is always nil or the failure is truly irrelevant, but that should be obvious from the type or explained near the discard. In application code I prefer an explicit check, even if the chosen action is a comment and best-effort continuation. Silence should be a reviewed policy, not a convenience.

sections.title: A zero value cannot explain how it was produced
sections.content:
Once the error is removed, downstream code sees only data. It cannot distinguish a legitimate zero from a fallback zero, a complete buffer from a short write, or a missing resource from an empty one. The causal link has been erased.

Handling near the call preserves context and gives tests a clear branch. When best-effort behavior is required, record that policy explicitly and consider metrics or logging at the owning boundary so repeated failures do not disappear unnoticed.

sections.title: What `_` hides
sections.content:
| Call | Result after failure | Risk when error is discarded |
|---|---|---|
| `strconv.Atoi` | `0` | Invalid input looks like a valid number |
| `os.Open` | nil file | Later method call can panic |
| `Writer.Write` | short count | Output can be incomplete |
| `Flush` or `Close` | existing object | Buffered data loss may go unnoticed |

sections.title: Keep a failed conversion from becoming valid data
